overview: Tyler's Law asks the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to look at whether hospital emergency rooms should routinely test overdose patients for fentanyl, a powerful synthetic opioid. Within three years, HHS must study how often ERs test for fentanyl and related drugs, when they don't, what it costs, the benefits and risks to patients, staff training needs, patient privacy, and barriers to testing. Within nine months after that study, HHS must issue guidance on whether fentanyl testing should be standard for overdose patients and how hospitals can make sure doctors know what their routine drug tests do and don't detect. The guidance is advice, not a requirement. As of March 24, 2026, it had passed the Senate and was waiting at the House desk.
for: Supporters say many standard hospital drug screens can miss fentanyl, and clear federal guidance could help doctors identify what caused an overdose and give patients better follow-up care.
against: Critics say the bill only orders a study and voluntary guidance, so it could take years to have any effect and still leave hospitals to decide on their own.
